## Recap: time series {.slide-your-turn .smaller}

**Select all statements that are true.**

- (A) A forecasting split should respect the order in which data become available.
- (B) Ordinary shuffled cross-validation is always appropriate for forecasting.
- (C) Forecasts can incorporate variables other than past target values.
- (D) A random forest using only a time feature can extrapolate a rising trend beyond the training range.

::: {.notes}
Answers: A and C. Trees predict using training-region leaf values, so a time-only forest does not extrapolate the trend.
:::

## When will a customer leave?

A telecom retention team wants to anticipate **time to churn**.

- **Event:** a customer leaves the service.
- **Time origin:** the customer’s signup.
- **Prediction:** a probability of staying beyond a relevant duration.

Timing can help plan outreach. Predicting churn does not tell us whether an offer will prevent it.

## Same duration, different information

| Customer | Observed months | Churn observed? | What we know |
|---|---:|---|---|
| A | 4 | Yes | Churn at month 4 |
| B | 4 | No | Stayed beyond month 4 |
| C | 18 | No | Stayed beyond month 18 |

**B and C have incomplete lifetimes, not zero churn risk.**

## Observation ends before the event

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.8))
for y, (customer, duration, observed) in enumerate(
    [("A", 4, True), ("B", 4, False), ("C", 18, False)]
):
    ax.hlines(y, 0, duration, color="tab:blue", linewidth=3)
    ax.plot(duration, y, "X" if observed else "o", color="tab:blue",
            markerfacecolor="tab:blue" if observed else "white", markersize=9)
    ax.text(duration + 0.6, y, "Churn" if observed else "Observation ends", va="center")
ax.set(yticks=[0, 1, 2], yticklabels=["A", "B", "C"],
       xlabel="Months since each customer's signup", xlim=(-0.5, 26), ylim=(-0.5, 2.5))
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_title("An observed event and two incomplete lifetimes")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Open circles mark the end of observation, not churn. Timelines align by time since signup, not calendar date.
:::

## Right-censoring

For a right-censored customer, we know a **lower bound** on time to churn.

- We observed them event-free through their recorded duration.
- We do not know their eventual churn time.
- We should preserve both the **duration** and **event indicator**.

The same structure appears in time to equipment failure or time until finding a job.

## Meet the customer data {.smaller}

[Telco Customer Churn](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/blastchar/telco-customer-churn): one row per customer.

| Column | Meaning in our teaching example |
|---|---|
| `tenure` | Months from signup to churn or the end of observation |
| `Churn` | Whether departure was observed (`Yes` / `No`) |
| `Contract` | Recorded contract type |
| `MonthlyCharges` | Recorded monthly charge |
| `InternetService` | Recorded internet service type |

**Teaching assumption:** this is a snapshot, not a documented customer history. We interpret `Churn = No` as right censoring.

::: {.notes}
Before operational use, verify sampling, follow-up, and which features were available at prediction time. Current contract and billing attributes need not be their values at signup. The demo inspects actual rows and explores data quality; these are model illustrations, not validated deployment predictions.
:::

## Could we use classification? {.smaller}

A snapshot label, “churn observed,” mixes customers with different follow-up lengths.

A fixed-horizon question can work: **Will they churn within six months of signup?**

| Record | Six-month label |
|---|---|
| Churn at month 4 | Positive |
| Active through month 8 | Negative |
| Observation ends at month 2, no churn | Unknown |

**An unknown horizon label cannot simply be labelled negative.**

## Two tempting shortcuts {.slide-your-turn}

1. Fit a regressor using **only customers who churned**.
2. Fit a regressor treating **every recorded tenure as final**.

A customer is still subscribed when observation ends at month 15.

**What information does each shortcut lose or misrepresent?**

::: {.notes}
Shortcut 1 discards evidence that this customer survived beyond 15 months. Shortcut 2 invents an event at month 15. Replacing their duration with the mean of observed events also discards the lower-bound information.
:::

## Why the shortcuts fail

**Events only:** selects customers whose events happened during follow-up; discards censored customers’ evidence of longer survival.

- Generally biases lifetime estimates downward under independent censoring.

**Follow-up as lifetime:** declares that active customers churned when observation ended.

- Learns observed follow-up rather than time to churn.

**Changing regressors does not repair the targets.**

## Preserve the two-part outcome

| Customer | `tenure` | `event` | What we know |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| A | 4 | 1 | Churn at month 4 |
| B | 4 | 0 | Stayed beyond month 4 |
| C | 18 | 0 | Stayed beyond month 18 |

- `event = 1`: churn observed (`Churn = Yes`).
- `event = 0`: churn not observed (`Churn = No`).

Duration and event status form the **outcome**, not the predictors.

::: {.notes}
The demo creates the numeric event column expected by lifelines. Zero means event not observed, not zero future churn risk. Both parts of the outcome matter: B contributes evidence of survival through month 4 even though their eventual churn time is unknown.
:::

## What should we predict instead?

The **survival function** describes the probability of staying beyond a duration:

$$S(t)=P(T>t)$$

If $S(12)=0.8$, the probability of staying **beyond 12 months from signup** is 0.8.

This is different from staying **another** 12 months for a customer who is already subscribed.

::: {.notes}
T is time from signup to churn. Survival means remaining with the service. We will read estimated survival curves in the demo rather than predicting a completed lifetime for every customer. No Kaplan–Meier calculation is required before the handoff.
:::

## After the demo: what would you tell the team? {.slide-your-turn}

A group has lower estimated retention, and the model predicts higher churn risk for some customers.

- What does a survival curve’s value at 12 months mean?
- Do the group curves show that changing a contract would prevent churn?
- Is predicted churn risk enough to decide whom to contact?

::: {.notes}
Return here after the demo. The curve measures survival beyond 12 months from signup, not another 12 months from today. Group differences and model coefficients describe associations. An outreach decision also needs evidence of intervention effectiveness, costs, and customer value; high predicted risk is not the same as high treatment benefit.
:::

## What did we learn? {.slide-summary}

- Censored records contain useful **partial information**.
- Preserve **duration and event status**.
- Familiar targets can discard information or invent event times.
- Survival curves describe retention across durations.
- Group comparisons and model predictions do not establish intervention effects.

**Define the event, time origin, and prediction time first.**
